title: Best Free AI Stylist Apps and Tools for Outfits (2026)
h1: Free AI stylist apps and tools for outfit advice in 2026
excerpt: Free AI stylist options for 2026: chatbots that read photos of your clothes, wardrobe apps with free AI, prompts that work, and the privacy trade-offs.
tldr: The best free AI stylist for most people is a chatbot you already use, such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude, all of which accept photos of your clothes on free plans with usage limits. For daily outfits from what you own, a wardrobe app with free AI, such as Alta, GetWardrobe or Acloset, keeps a catalogue that a chatbot doesn't.
body:
The best free AI stylist for most people is a general chatbot. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude all accept photos on their free plans, with usage limits, and can answer questions about colour, dress codes and what goes with what. For daily outfit suggestions from clothes you own, a wardrobe app with free AI features works better, because it remembers your wardrobe: Alta is free, and GetWardrobe and Acloset are free for up to 100 items.

This guide covers both routes, with prompts that get useful answers, where the free tiers stop and what happens to the photos you upload. Tools are described from their official websites, help pages and store listings, checked in October 2026; we haven't tested them ourselves, and free limits change often.

Looking for AI that designs the wardrobe itself, as in a cupboard or fitted closet? That's interior design software. This guide is about the clothes that go inside.

Free chatbots as a stylist: ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude

Any of the three can look at a photo of an outfit or a few garments and tell you what works, suggest combinations from a list you type out, explain a dress code or draft a capsule wardrobe. The differences are mostly in limits and privacy settings.

ChatGPT

OpenAI's free tier FAQ says free users can upload images in their prompts, and its pricing page lists "Limited messages with uploads" for the Free plan. It doesn't publish exact caps, so a long session with lots of photos can run into the limit.

Gemini

Google's Gemini help page says you need to be signed in to upload files, including photos, with up to 10 files per prompt "subject to availability" and higher limits on Google AI Pro and Ultra. Free caps aren't stated.

Claude

Anthropic's help page on uploads covers JPEG, PNG, GIF and WebP images, up to 20 files per chat, and names no plan restriction. The free plan's usage limits vary rather than being a fixed number.

The catch with all three is memory. A chatbot sees the photos in the current chat, not your wardrobe, and unless you use a memory or project feature, each new chat starts from nothing. Keep a short text list of your main pieces (navy wool coat, grey sweatshirt, dark straight-leg jeans, white leather trainers and so on) and paste it in when you ask.

Wardrobe apps with free AI features

These keep a catalogue of your clothes, so suggestions come only from what you own. Our full list of the best digital wardrobe apps covers each one in more depth, along with apps that don't use AI.

Alta: free AI outfit suggestions

Alta lists no paid tier: its website says "Alta is free to use", and the US App Store showed no in-app purchases in October 2026. It suggests outfits each day from the weather and your schedule, styles named events and builds outfits around a piece you choose, with avatar try-on. It also has shopping features, such as price-drop alerts, and runs on iPhone, iPad, Android and the web.

GetWardrobe: 100 items and an outfit generator

GetWardrobe's free tier covers up to 100 items (clothes and outfits counted together). It includes AI background removal, unlimited use of its AI Studio and a starter AI Outfit Generator that makes 10 outfits per run, filtered by weather, occasion and mood. It syncs across phones, Mac and the web.

Acloset: every feature up to 100 items

Acloset's website says all its features are free for up to 100 items. Those features include an AI stylist chat, daily outfit suggestions based on the weather and your schedule, and colour and fit analysis. The free version shows ads, and the App Store also lists credit packs, so check what each AI feature uses.

Fits: unlimited items, capped AI

Fits is free with unlimited items and background removal. Its AI stylist chat suggests outfits by style, weather and occasion, but unlimited AI suggestions need Fits Pro, and extra AI credits are sold separately, so expect a cap without paying.

Cladwell: AI chat with usage limits

Cladwell is free to download with basic use. It has an AI chat stylist, "Ask Cladwell", and its site says AI features have usage limits; a subscription with a 7-day trial covers the rest. You can add clothes from its catalogue rather than photographing them, and its FAQ says photos aren't used to train AI.

Google Photos Wardrobe: free if you're eligible

In the US, Brazil and India, Google Photos can build a wardrobe from photos of you, let you mix outfits of up to six items and preview them on you. It's part of the free app, but Google's help page says it's rolling out to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers "as well as other select users", and non-subscribers need more than 1,000 photos of themselves.

Three others are worth knowing about for what they don't give away. Indyx is free with unlimited items but uses AI only to tag clothes, by design; it sells human stylists instead. Pureple's Android app keeps its Style Me AI suggestions for Pureple Pro. Whering is free, and an October 2026 iPhone update says its planner now suggests outfits from your wardrobe and the weather, though its Outfit Maker is a paid extra.

Example prompts for free AI outfit suggestions

Vague questions get vague answers. Give the AI what a stylist would ask for: the occasion, the weather, the dress code, what you own and what you won't wear. These work in any of the chatbots above.

Outfits from what you own

"Here are photos of 12 pieces from my wardrobe. Suggest three outfits for a smart-casual office day, around 12°C (54°F) with rain likely. Use only these pieces, say which shoes to wear, and give one line on why each outfit works."

Building around one piece

"I own a rust corduroy overshirt. My other clothes: [paste your list]. Give me four outfits built around it: a weekend walk, a casual dinner, a video call and a cold-weather version."

A capsule wardrobe from your own clothes

"Here's everything I own for autumn, with colours: [list]. Pick 30 pieces that mix well into a capsule wardrobe, list ten outfits they make, and name at most two gaps worth filling. Don't suggest buying anything that adds fewer than five new outfits."

New to capsules? Read what a capsule wardrobe is and how to build one first, then use the AI to check your picks.

A colour check

"Photo attached: a navy blazer with olive chinos. Do these colours work together? If not, which of these would: charcoal wool trousers, stone chinos or black jeans?"

Decoding a dress code

"The invitation says 'smart casual' for an outdoor summer party. What does that usually mean, and what are two versions I could wear using these pieces: [list]?"

Two habits improve the answers. Ask for a reason with every suggestion, so you can spot advice that doesn't fit your life. And ask it to say when it isn't sure of a colour in a photo, since indoor lighting shifts colours a lot.

Can AI pick your outfits?

Partly. AI handles the mechanical side of getting dressed well enough, and struggles with anything that depends on your body, your day or your taste.

What it does well:

  • Pairing colours and spotting clashes, especially from a clear photo
  • Finding combinations you haven't tried from a long list of pieces
  • Explaining dress codes such as business casual or cocktail
  • Drafting a capsule wardrobe or packing list from what you own (our guide shows how to build a capsule wardrobe with AI)

What it does badly:

  • Fit and fabric. It can't feel that a wool jumper is too warm for a heated office or see that trousers shrank in the wash.
  • Colour from poor photos. Warm indoor light can make navy look black and cream look yellow.
  • Your context: the unwritten rules at work, the bike ride to the station, the colour you'd never wear.
  • Sticking to your wardrobe. Chatbots can slip in pieces you never mentioned, so tell them to use only what you've listed.

Shopping apps have added AI search, styling and try-on too, but those features are built to help you buy, not to style what you already have.

For a big occasion or a full wardrobe overhaul, a human stylist who can see you in person still has the edge. Some wardrobe apps sell that as a service; Indyx, for one, lists virtual stylist sessions from $60.

Where free AI styling stops

Every free option has limits, and they're rarely given as numbers.

  • Message and upload caps. ChatGPT's Free plan has limited messages with uploads, Gemini allows up to 10 files per prompt subject to availability, and Claude's free limits vary. None of the pages checked gives a fixed daily number for free users.
  • Item caps. Acloset and GetWardrobe stop at 100 items, and GetWardrobe counts saved outfits towards that.
  • AI caps and credits. Fits keeps unlimited AI suggestions for Fits Pro, GetWardrobe's free generator makes 10 outfits per run and Cladwell's AI has usage limits. Several apps sell credits for try-on and image features.
  • Ads and shopping. Acloset's free version shows ads, and Alta and Fits include shopping suggestions. When an app is free, it's worth asking how it makes money.

Privacy: what happens to the photos you upload

Photos of clothes often show more than clothes: your face in a mirror, your bedroom, sometimes the view from your window. Each service treats them differently.

  • ChatGPT: OpenAI says it may use content from Free, Plus and Pro accounts to train its models. You can turn this off with Improve the model for everyone under Settings, then Data controls. Temporary chats aren't used to improve its models and may be kept for up to 30 days for safety.
  • Gemini: with Keep Activity on, Google says a subset of chats is reviewed by humans and uploaded photos are used to improve its services with their help, and it asks you not to enter confidential information you wouldn't want a reviewer to see. Temporary chats, and chats with Keep Activity off, are kept with your account for 72 hours and aren't used to train its models unless you send feedback.
  • Claude: Anthropic says it uses consumer chats to improve its models only if you allow it through the Model Improvement privacy setting, or if a chat is flagged for safety review. Incognito chats aren't used.
  • Wardrobe apps: many sync your closet through an online account, so your photos sit on the company's servers. The App Store's App Privacy section and Google Play's Data safety section show what each app collects and shares; Whering's Google Play listing, for example, says it may share photos and videos with third parties.

FitWardrobe is our app, and it isn't available yet. When it opens on Android and the web, it will store your wardrobe on your device. To tag a piece it will send a compressed photo to Google's Gemini API, and to suggest an outfit it will send item details to Groq, so the AI features need an internet connection. The AI transparency page sets out the details.

A few habits help with any tool. Photograph clothes flat or on a hanger rather than on you, crop out faces and rooms, and switch off location tagging in your camera settings if you don't want it saved in your photos. Our guide on how to digitise your wardrobe covers taking clean photos, and the downsides and privacy risks of wardrobe apps go further.

faq.q: What is the best free AI for fashion advice?
faq.a: For questions, a general chatbot is the best free option. ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude all accept photos of outfits on their free plans, with usage limits, and can explain colours, dress codes and combinations. For daily outfits from your own clothes, a wardrobe app with free AI, such as Alta, keeps a catalogue that a chatbot doesn't. Free limits change, so check each plan.

faq.q: Is there a free AI wardrobe app?
faq.a: Yes. Alta is free, lists no in-app purchases and suggests outfits daily with AI. GetWardrobe and Acloset are free for up to 100 items, with AI outfit features, and Fits is free with unlimited items but caps AI suggestions without Fits Pro. In the US, Brazil and India, Google Photos Wardrobe builds a closet from your photos for eligible users.

faq.q: Is there a free AI outfit generator that uses my own clothes?
faq.a: Yes, two kinds. A free chatbot such as ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude will suggest outfits from photos or a list of your clothes, within its usage limits, if you tell it to use only what you've listed. Wardrobe apps with free AI features, such as Alta, GetWardrobe and Acloset, keep a catalogue of your clothes and suggest outfits from it, with limits on items or features that vary by app.

faq.q: Can ChatGPT suggest outfits from photos of my clothes?
faq.a: Yes. ChatGPT's free plan accepts image uploads, with a limited number of messages that include them. Photograph a few pieces clearly in daylight, give the occasion and the weather, and ask it to use only what's in the photos. A new chat won't remember your wardrobe unless you use a memory feature, so keep a text list of your main pieces to paste in.

faq.q: Can AI make a capsule wardrobe for free?
faq.a: Yes, a free chatbot can draft one. List what you own with colours, describe a typical week and your climate, and ask it to pick 25 to 35 pieces that mix well and to name any real gaps. Ask for a set of outfits to prove the pieces work together, then check the result against your wardrobe, since AI can't judge fit or wear.

faq.q: Is it safe to upload photos of my clothes to AI?
faq.a: It can be, if you control what's in the photo and check the settings. Crop out faces and rooms first. ChatGPT has an Improve the model for everyone switch, Gemini has Keep Activity, and Claude asks whether chats can be used for model improvement. Wardrobe apps often store photos in an online account, and their store privacy labels show what's shared.

faq.q: Can AI replace a human stylist?
faq.a: Not fully. AI is good at pairing colours, finding new combinations and explaining dress codes, and free tools are available at any hour. It can't see how clothes fit you, feel fabric or read an occasion the way a person in the room can. For a wedding outfit or a full wardrobe overhaul, a human stylist still adds the most.
